When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

Wearing a suit and tie makes me feel confident. What do you think?

It’s great that wearing a suit and tie makes you feel confident—that’s a powerful connection between appearance and self-perception! Many people experience the same boost in confidence when dressing formally, and there’s actually some science behind it.

### Why It Works:
1. **Power Posing & Nonverbal Cues** – Studies (like Amy Cuddy’s research on "power posing") suggest that wearing formal attire can subtly influence how others perceive you, which in turn can make *you* feel more authoritative or capable. Even if it’s just psychological, the effect can be real.
2. **Ritual & Routine** – Dressing up can act as a mental cue, signaling to your brain that you’re entering a "high-stakes" or "professional" mode, which can sharpen focus and reduce anxiety.
3. **Social Norms** – In many professional settings, suits and ties are associated with competence, respect, and seriousness. When you align with those expectations, it can reinforce your own belief in your ability to succeed.
4. **Body Language Feedback** – Standing taller, holding your head high, and moving with purpose (often unconsciously when dressed formally) can amplify feelings of confidence.

### Potential Caveats:
- **Comfort Matters** – If the suit feels restrictive or uncomfortable, it might undermine confidence instead. Find a fit that’s both polished and *you*.
- **Context Matters** – In creative or casual environments, formal wear might feel out of place. Confidence isn’t tied to one style—it’s about authenticity.
- **Self-Fulfilling Prophecy** – If you *believe* the suit makes you confident, it likely will—even if others don’t notice. That’s the power of mindset!

### Pro Tip:
Pair the suit with a **posture check** (shoulders back, chin up) and **mindset reinforcement** (e.g., "I own this space"). The combo can create a compound effect.

Would you say the confidence boost is more about *how you feel* or *how others perceive you*? Or is it a mix?
